name: Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy

criteria.description: Progressive or relapsing symmetric proximal and distal weakness and sensory dysfunction of all extremities developing over at least 8 weeks
Absent or reduced deep tendon reflexes in all limbs
Electrodiagnostic evidence of demyelination in motor nerves (prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction velocities, conduction block, temporal dispersion)
MRI showing nerve root/plexus hypertrophy and/or enhancement

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Clinical criteria plus electrodiagnostic evidence of demyelination in at least 2 motor nerves. Supportive criteria strengthen the diagnosis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Atypical CIDP variants include distal (DADS), multifocal (Lewis-Sumner/MADSAM), focal, motor-predominant, and sensory-predominant forms. Anti-NF155, anti-CNTN1, and anti-Caspr1 antibodies define autoimmune nodopathies.

searchTerms: blockage of nerve signals to muscles

pathognomonic.symptomName: Fatiguable weakness of proximal limb muscles
searchTerms: weakness in upper arms and thighs that worsens with use
muscle tiredness in shoulders and hips
proximal muscle weakness that gets worse with activity
immune response to nerve adhesion molecule 186
immune reaction to nerve adhesion protein
immune attack on nerve adhesion complex

laboratory: Elevated CSF protein (typically >45 mg/dL) with normal cell count
Anti-NF155, anti-CNTN1, anti-Caspr1 antibodies in nodopathy subset
Paraprotein screening (SPEP, immunofixation) to exclude paraprotein-associated neuropathy
imaging: MRI of brachial/lumbosacral plexus showing nerve root hypertrophy and enhancement
Ultrasound showing nerve enlargement (cross-sectional area increase)
genetic: No causative genetic factors for typical CIDP
Genetic testing may be needed to exclude hereditary demyelinating neuropathies (CMT1)
other: Nerve conduction studies showing demyelinating features: prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction velocities, conduction block, temporal dispersion, prolonged F-wave latencies
Sural nerve biopsy showing onion-bulb formation and segmental demyelination (rarely needed)
Response to immunotherapy (IVIg, corticosteroids, or plasma exchange) supports diagnosis

distinguishingFeatures: GBS reaches nadir within 4 weeks; CIDP progresses beyond 8 weeks
GBS is typically monophasic; CIDP is chronic/relapsing
CMT has family history and lifelong slowly progressive course
CMT has uniformly slow conduction velocities without conduction block
CMT does not respond to immunotherapy
MMN is purely motor without sensory involvement
MMN does not respond to corticosteroids

redFlags: Failure to respond to standard immunotherapy should prompt reconsideration of diagnosis
Purely motor presentation may indicate multifocal motor neuropathy
Uniform conduction slowing without conduction block suggests hereditary neuropathy
Monoclonal gammopathy must be excluded (MGUS, POEMS, lymphoma)
Rapid progression resembling GBS but evolving beyond 8 weeks
Young patients with anti-NF155 antibodies have distinct phenotype with tremor and ataxia
references: Van den Bergh PYK, et al. European Academy of Neurology/Peripheral Nerve Society guideline on diagnosis and treatment of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Eur J Neurol. 2021;28(11):3556-3583.
Lehmann HC, et al. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy: update on diagnosis, immunopathogenesis and treatment. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry. 2019;90(9):981-987.
Querol L, et al. Antibodies against peripheral nerve antigens in chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Sci Rep. 2023.
